summary: Provides guidelines for operators of 6bone routing equipment to follow for efficient and stable routing in that IPv6 test network. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2772 sets routing and operating guidelines for the 6Bone, an IPv6 testbed. It tells participating sites which routes to advertise, how to maintain registry and DNS information, and how to handle problems.

subtitle: Routing rules written for stability across the 6Bone IPv6 testbed.

tldr.problem: The 6Bone was an IPv6 testbed whose backbone needed consistent routing practices to remain stable as it grew.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets rules for special address prefixes, route aggregation, the site registry, joining the testbed, pTLA qualification, and handling operational problems.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2546 and has been updated by RFC 3152; its guidance describes the 6Bone in 2000.

today: RFC 2772 is Informational, obsoletes RFC 2546, and has been updated by RFC 3152. Its routing and operating guidance describes the 6Bone testbed in 2000.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
The 6Bone was an IPv6 testbed intended to help IPv6 evolve and be deployed. The document gives best-practice guidance to operators of routing equipment under the testbed's IPv6 allocation, with the goal of maintaining an efficient and stable backbone.

The RFC names BGP-4 with Multiprotocol Extensions, commonly called BGP4+, as the accepted exterior gateway protocol at the time. Its requirement words, including MUST and SHOULD, have the meanings assigned by RFC 2119.
sections.plainLanguage: The 6Bone was a test network for IPv6. These guidelines told its operators how to manage routes so that problems at one site would not destabilize the shared backbone.

sections.title: Special Prefixes and Default Routes
sections.content:
The RFC restricts advertisements of address ranges that should not appear in ordinary backbone routing. Link-local prefixes FE80::/10, loopback ::1/128, and unspecified ::0/128 MUST NOT be advertised. Site-local FEC0::/10 may be advertised inside a site but MUST NOT cross transit pNLAs, pTLAs, or leaf sites.

Multicast prefixes MUST NOT be advertised through unicast routing, and link-local and node-local multicast must not be routed. IPv4-compatible prefixes SHOULD NOT be used or routed; EGPs MUST NOT advertise them to transit pNLAs or pTLAs. IPv4-mapped prefixes may be advertised by an IGP inside a site but MUST NOT be advertised by an EGP. Core pTLA routers MUST be default-free, and undefined unicast prefixes outside 2000::/3 MUST NOT be advertised.
sections.plainLanguage: Some address ranges are restricted to a local link or site. The rules keep them, along with loopback and unspecified addresses, out of backbone route advertisements.

sections.title: Route Aggregation and Peering
sections.content:
Border routers using an exterior gateway protocol with other IPv6 sites MUST aggregate routes. They MUST NOT leak more-specific routes into or across the 6Bone backbone. A leaf site or pNLA must advertise to an upstream provider only prefixes assigned by that provider.

Site border routers MUST NOT advertise prefixes longer than their upstream allocation. 6Bone pTLAs MUST NOT advertise prefixes longer than a pTLA delegation, then specified as /24 or /28, to other pTLAs unless they have a special peering arrangement. Even under such an arrangement, the more-specific routes must not leak to non-participating pTLAs or downstream sites.

The 6Bone prefix is 3FFE::/16. The RFC says some routing rules were expected to apply to newer TLA allocations as well, while leaving peering details to the networks involved.
sections.plainLanguage: Each site should announce only the routes it received from its provider. Aggregation keeps detailed routes from spreading across the backbone, except for the limited arrangements described in the RFC.

sections.title: Registry and Joining Requirements
sections.content:
Each 6Bone site, pNLA, and pTLA MUST maintain registry entries describing the site, each prefix delegation, and a contact for maintenance or administration. The contact entry must refer to a person or role record, which may be kept in another Internet registry.

A new site should connect to a transit pNLA or pTLA in its region and MUST maintain DNS for forward and reverse lookups. Its upstream provider must delegate the reverse DNS zone to the site or agree to operate primary DNS, and must create the registry entry for the delegated address space.
sections.plainLanguage: A participating site had to keep its address and contact details in the registry and maintain forward and reverse DNS. The upstream provider also had responsibilities for the delegated address space.

sections.title: pTLA Qualification and Problem Handling
sections.content:
An applicant for a pTLA allocation needed at least three months of qualifying experience as a 6Bone end site or pNLA transit. The applicant also needed maintained registry and DNS entries, reliable BGP4+ connectivity, an IPv6-reachable service description, at least two support staff with three preferred, a shared support mailbox, a potential user community, and a commitment to follow the operational rules. The 6Bone Operations Group assessed applications and monitored compliance.

Participation was voluntary, but sites were expected to follow the guidelines. A site that found a problem SHOULD first contact the maintainer through the registry, then raise unresolved matters with the Operations Group. If a problem caused major operational disruption, backbone sites SHOULD consider temporary filters to restore service.
sections.plainLanguage: A pTLA applicant had to show operating experience, reliable connectivity, support staff, and a commitment to the rules. When problems arose, the RFC recommended contacting the site first and escalating unresolved issues.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says incorrect routes usually make sites unreachable. Aggregating and rejecting routes under the guidelines was expected to make routing less sensitive to denial-of-service attacks that use misleading routes.

The 6Bone was a testbed, so denial of service and packet disclosure were expected risks. The pTLA from which an attack originated had ultimate responsibility for isolating and fixing it. Sites were also responsible for introducing test systems where bugs or misconfiguration would have minimal effect on others.
sections.plainLanguage: Incorrect routes can make sites unreachable and can support denial-of-service attacks. The RFC assigns responsibility for fixing an attack to the originating pTLA and says test systems should be placed to limit harm.
